summary: Bump-in-the-Host (BIH) is a host-based IPv4-to-IPv6 translation mechanism that lets IPv4-only applications that work through NATs communicate with IPv6-only peers. It hides IPv6 by locally synthesizing IPv4 addresses. The host may be on an IPv6-only or dual-stack network.

plainLanguage.summary: Some programs only understand the older kind of IP address, but the server they need to reach only answers over IPv6. Bump-in-the-Host solves this inside the computer: it answers the program's name lookup with a made-up IPv4 address that only means something locally, and then swaps that address for the server's real IPv6 address when the packets go out.

subtitle: A translator inside a host that lets IPv4-only programs reach IPv6-only servers by handing out local IPv4 addresses.

tldr.problem: Some IPv4-only applications still need to reach servers that are reachable only over IPv6, from hosts on IPv6-only or dual-stack networks.
tldr.mechanism: Bump-in-the-Host intercepts the application's name lookups and socket calls, hands the application a synthetic private IPv4 address mapped to the server's real IPv6 address, and translates the traffic either at the socket API or at the IP layer.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6535 combines and obsoletes RFC 2767 and RFC 3338 and puts the technology on the Standards Track. The socket API variant is recommended. Using BIH together with a NAT64 is NOT RECOMMENDED.

facts.label: IPv4 MTU
facts.value: MTU of the IPv6 enabled link minus 20 bytes

today: RFC 6535 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2012. It obsoletes RFC 2767 and RFC 3338, and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: What Bump-in-the-Host Does
sections.content:
Bump-in-the-Host (BIH) is a host-based IPv4 to IPv6 protocol translation mechanism that allows a class of IPv4-only applications that work through NATs to communicate with IPv6-only peers. The host on which the applications run may be connected to IPv6-only or dual-stack access networks. BIH hides IPv6 and makes the IPv4-only applications think they are talking with IPv4 peers, by the local synthesis of IPv4 addresses.

The document describes BIH as the successor and combination of the Bump-in-the-Stack (BIS) and Bump-in-the-API (BIA) techniques of RFC 2767 and RFC 3338, which enable IPv4-only legacy applications to communicate with IPv6-only servers by synthesizing IPv4 addresses from AAAA records.

The supported class of applications includes those that use DNS for IP address resolution and that do not embed IP address literals in application-protocol payloads. This includes legacy client-server applications that are agnostic to the IP address family used by the destination and that are able to do NAT traversal. The synthetic IPv4 addresses shown to applications are taken from the private address pool of RFC 1918, in order to ensure that possible NAT traversal techniques will be initiated.

The IETF recommends using solutions based on dual stack or tunnelling for IPv6 transition, and specifically recommends against deployments that use double protocol translation. Use of BIH together with a NAT64 is NOT RECOMMENDED.

BIH has two major implementation alternatives: a protocol translator between the IPv4 and the IPv6 stacks of a host, or an API translator between the IPv4 socket API module and the TCP/IP module. Essentially, IPv4 is translated into IPv6 at the socket API layer or at the IP layer, and the socket API layer is the recommended implementation alternative. When BIH is implemented at the socket API layer, the translator intercepts IPv4 socket API function calls and invokes corresponding IPv6 socket API function calls to communicate with IPv6 hosts. When BIH is implemented at the network layer, the IPv4 packets are intercepted and converted to IPv6 using the IP conversion mechanism defined in SIIT, with the same benefits and drawbacks as SIIT.

The location of the BIH refers to the location of the protocol translation function. The location of the IPv4 address and DNS A record synthesis function is orthogonal to the location of the protocol translation, and may or may not happen at the same place. BIH can be used whenever an IPv4-only application needs to communicate with an IPv6-only server, independently of the address families supported by the access network, so the access network can be IPv6-only or dual-stack capable.
sections.plainLanguage: BIH is a translator that runs inside the computer, not in the network. It is meant for programs that find their server through a name lookup and never write an IP address into the data they send, which is what lets the translator sit between the program and the network.

sections.title: The Parts of BIH
sections.content:
Dual-stack hosts, as defined in RFC 4213, need applications, TCP/IP modules and addresses for both IPv4 and IPv6. The hosts proposed in this document add an API or network-layer translator so that legacy IPv4 applications can communicate with IPv6-only peers.

The BIH architecture consists of an Extension Name Resolver, an address mapper, and, depending on the implementation, either a function mapper or a protocol translator. The placement of the Extension Name Resolver is orthogonal to the placement of the protocol translation: the Extension Name Resolver may reside in the socket API while protocol translation takes place at the network layer.

The choice between the socket API and network-layer architectures varies case by case. While the socket API architecture alternative is the recommended one, it may not always be possible to choose. That may be the case, for example, when the operating system used does not allow modifications for API implementations but does allow the addition of virtual network interfaces and related software modules. On the other hand, sometimes it may not be possible to introduce protocol translators inside the operating system, but it may be easy to modify implementations behind the API provided for applications. The choice also depends on who is creating the implementation: an application framework provider, an operating system provider and a device vendor may all choose different approaches because of their different positions.

The function mapper translates an IPv4 socket API function into an IPv6 socket API function. When detecting IPv4 socket API function calls from IPv4 applications, it MUST intercept the function calls and invoke IPv6 socket API functions that correspond to the IPv4 socket API functions. It MUST NOT perform function mapping when the application is initiating communications to the address range used by local synthesis and the address mapping table does not have an entry matching the address.

The protocol translator translates IPv4 into IPv6 and vice versa, using the IP conversion mechanism defined in SIIT. To avoid unnecessary fragmentation, the host's IPv4 module SHOULD be configured with a small enough MTU, that is the MTU of the IPv6 enabled link minus 20 bytes. Protocol translation cannot be performed for IPv4 packets sent to the IPv4 address range used by local synthesis when no mapping table entry exists, and the implementation SHOULD attempt to route such packets via IPv4 interfaces instead.
sections.plainLanguage: BIH has three working parts. One answers the program's name lookup, one hands out and remembers the local IPv4 addresses, and one either rewrites the program's socket calls or rewrites the packets. The name lookup part and the translation part may sit in different places in the system.

sections.title: How a Name Becomes an Address
sections.content:
The Extension Name Resolver (ENR) returns an answer in response to the IPv4 application's name resolution request.

In the socket API-layer implementation, when an IPv4 application tries to do a forward lookup to resolve names via the resolver library, for example with gethostbyname(), BIH intercepts the function call and instead calls the IPv6 equivalent functions, for example getaddrinfo(), that resolve both A and AAAA records. This implementation alternative is name resolution protocol agnostic, so it supports techniques such as a hosts file, NetBIOS and mDNS, and anything else the underlying operating system uses.

In the network-layer implementation, the ENR intercepts the A query and creates an additional AAAA query with similar content. The ENR then collects replies to both queries and, depending on the results, either returns an A reply unmodified or synthesizes a new A reply. If no reply for the A query is received after an ENR-implementation-specific timeout, and after a positive AAAA response, the ENR MAY choose to proceed as if there were only an AAAA record available for the destination. This alternative can only catch name resolution requests that result in actual DNS queries, so it is more limited than the socket API-layer alternative, and for that reason the socket API-layer alternative is RECOMMENDED.

In either implementation, if a DNS A record reply contains non-excluded real IPv4 addresses, the ENR MUST NOT synthesize IPv4 addresses. The ENR asks the address mapper to assign a synthetic IPv4 address corresponding to each received IPv6 address if the A record query resulted in a negative response, all received real IPv4 addresses were excluded, or the A query timed out. The timeout value is implementation specific and may be short, in order to provide a good user experience. If the response contains a CNAME or a DNAME record, the CNAME or DNAME chain is followed until the first terminating A or AAAA record is reached.

The document summarises the behaviour in a table: an application asking for IPv4 addresses that are answered with IPv4 addresses gets the real IPv4 addresses back; an application asking for IPv4 addresses that is answered with IPv6 addresses gets synthetic IPv4 addresses; and an application asking for IPv4 addresses that is answered with both gets the real IPv4 addresses back.
sections.plainLanguage: The resolver answers the program's question. If the name has a real IPv4 address, that address is returned untouched. If the name only has an IPv6 address, the resolver asks the address mapper for a local IPv4 address and returns that instead, remembering the pairing so that later packets can be translated.

sections.title: The Address Mapper and Synthetic Addresses
sections.content:
The address mapper maintains an IPv4 address pool used for IPv4 address synthesis, consisting of the private IPv4 addresses of RFC 1918 as described in Section 4.4. It also maintains a table consisting of pairs of synthetic IPv4 addresses and the destinations' real IPv6 addresses.

When the ENR, the translator or the function mapper asks the address mapper to assign a synthetic IPv4 address corresponding to an IPv6 address, the address mapper selects and returns an IPv4 address out of the local pool and registers a new entry in the table. Registration occurs in three cases: when the ENR gets only IPv6 addresses for the target host name and there is no existing mapping entry for those IPv6 addresses; when the ENR gets both real IPv4 and IPv6 addresses but the real IPv4 addresses contain only excluded IPv4 addresses, such as 127.0.0.1, in which case the behaviour follows the first case; and when the function mapper is triggered by a received IPv6 packet and there is no existing mapping entry for the IPv6 source address, for example when a client sent a UDP request to an anycast address but a response arrived from a unicast address.

A synthetic IPv4 address is defined as an IPv4 address that has meaning only inside a host and that is used to provide an IPv4 representation of a remote node's real IPv6 address. A real IPv4 address is one the host has learned, for example from a DNS response to an A query, and a real IPv6 address is one learned, for example from a DNS response to a AAAA query.

An ENR implementation SHOULD, by default, exclude certain real IPv4 and IPv6 addresses seen on received A and AAAA records. The addresses excluded by default MAY include those that should not appear in the DNS or on the wire. Additional addresses MAY be excluded based on possibly configurable local policies.

Reverse lookups are handled by the ENR. When an application requests a reverse lookup for an IPv4 address, the ENR MUST check whether the queried address can be found in the address mapper's table and whether it is synthetic. If it is, the ENR MUST initiate a corresponding reverse lookup for the real IPv6 address and return the name received as the response to the application. A request for an address outside the synthetic pool, such as a global address, MUST be passed on unmodified.

DNS cache entries for synthetic IPv4 addresses MUST be flushed when BIH shuts down or when address mapping table entries are cleared. There may be a DNS cache in the network-layer ENR itself and at the host's stub resolver.
sections.plainLanguage: The address mapper is the memory of the translation. It hands out a local IPv4 address for each real IPv6 address it sees, keeps the two paired, and looks the pairing up again when traffic comes back the other way. The pairings must survive for a long time, because a program may hold on to the address it was given.

sections.title: The Address Pools
sections.content:
The address pool consists of the private IPv4 addresses of RFC 1918. It can be implemented at different granularities in the node, for example a single pool per node, or at some finer granularity such as per user or per process. In the case of a large number of IPv4 applications communicating with a large number of IPv6 servers, the available address space may be exhausted if the granularity is not fine enough. This should be a rare event, and the chances will decrease as IPv6 support increases. The applications may use the IPv4 addresses they learn for a much longer period than the DNS time to live indicates, so the mapping table entries should be kept active for a long period of time: a web browser may initiate one DNS query and then create multiple TCP sessions over time to the address it learns. When address mapping table clean-up is required, the BIH may use the techniques used by network address translators, as described in RFC 2663, RFC 5382 and RFC 5508.

The address space of RFC 1918 was chosen because legacy applications generally understand it as a private address space; a new dedicated address space would run the risk of not being understood by applications as private. 127/8 and 169.254/16 are rejected due to possible assumptions applications may make when seeing them.

The addresses of RFC 1918 used by the BIH have a risk of conflicting with addresses used in the host's possible IPv4 interfaces and corresponding local networks. The conflicts can be mitigated but not fully avoided by using less commonly used portions of the address space of RFC 1918; addresses from 172.16/12 are thought to be less likely to be in conflict than addresses from 10/8 or 192.168/16 spaces. A source address can usually be selected in a non-conflicting manner, but a small possibility exists for synthesized destination addresses being in conflict with real addresses used in attached IPv4 networks.

The recommended addresses are:

  • Primary source addresses: 172.21.112.0/20. Source addresses have to be allocated because applications use getsockname() calls and, in the network-layer mode, an IP address of the IPv4 interface has to be shown. More than one address is allocated to allow implementation flexibility, for example for a host with multiple IPv6 interfaces. The source addresses are from different subnets than the destination addresses, to ensure that applications do not make on-link assumptions and instead enable NAT traversal functions.
  • Secondary source addresses: 10.170.224.0/20. Recommended if a host has a conflict with the primary source addresses.
  • Primary destination addresses: 10.170.160.0/20. The address mapper selects destination addresses primarily out of this pool.
  • Secondary destination addresses: 172.21.80.0/20. The address mapper selects destination addresses out of this pool if the node has a dual-stack connection conflicting with the primary destination addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: The local addresses come from the private IPv4 ranges that old programs already treat as private. Two separate pools are used, one for the local end of a connection and one for the far end, and they are in different subnets so that a program does not assume the far end is on the same local network.

sections.title: Behaviour and Limits
sections.content:
IPv4 socket API functions are translated into IPv6 socket API functions that are semantically as identical as possible, and vice versa. Some IPv4 socket API functions are not fully compatible with IPv6, since IPv4 supports features that are not present in IPv6, such as SO_BROADCAST.

BIH SHOULD select a source address for a socket from the recommended source address pool if a socket used for communications has not been explicitly bound to any IPv4 address, and the binding of an explicitly bound socket MUST NOT be changed by BIH. ICMPv4 and ICMPv6 messages MUST be translated as defined by SIIT; in the network-layer implementation the protocol translator MUST translate ICMPv6 packets to ICMPv4 and vice versa, and in the socket API implementation the socket API MUST handle conversions in a similar fashion.

In the case of dual-stack destinations, BIH MUST NOT do protocol translation from IPv4 to IPv6 when the host has any IPv4 interfaces, native or tunnelled, available for use. It is possible that an IPv4 interface is activated during BIH operation, for example if a node moves into the coverage area of an IPv4-enabled network; in that event BIH MUST stop initiating protocol translation sessions for new connections, and BIH MAY disconnect active sessions. The choice of disconnection is left to implementations, and it may depend on whether an IPv4 address conflict occurs between addresses used by BIH and addresses used by the new IPv4 interface.

Protocol translation for multicast is not supported. No Application-Level Gateway functionality is specified, since ALG design is generally not encouraged for host-based translation and BIH is intended for applications that do not include IP addresses in protocol payloads.
sections.plainLanguage: Some IPv4 socket options have no IPv6 equivalent and are lost in translation. If the host later gains a working IPv4 connection, BIH must stop starting new translated connections, because the program can then use IPv4 directly.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of BIH follow closely, but not completely, those of NAT64 and DNS64.

Any protocols that protect IP header information are essentially incompatible with BIH. End-to-end IPsec verification will fail when the Authentication Header is used, in both transport and tunnel mode, and when ESP is used in transport mode. This is inherent in any network-layer translation mechanism. End-to-end IPsec protection can be restored using UDP encapsulation, as described in RFC 3948.

BIH creates binding state using packets flowing from the IPv4 side to the IPv6 side, and in accordance with the procedures defined in the document, a BIH implementation MUST offer Endpoint-Independent Mapping. Implementations MAY also provide support for Address-Dependent Mapping. The security properties, however, are determined by which packets the BIH allows in and which it does not, that is by the filtering behaviour and the possible filtering configuration, not by the address mapping behaviour.

The BIH implementation itself is a potential victim of different types of attacks, in particular denial-of-service attacks. The BIH has a limited number of IPv4 addresses that it uses to create the bindings, and even though it performs address translation, an attacker can consume the synthetic IPv4 address pool by triggering a host to issue DNS queries for names that cause the ENR to synthesize A records. Denial-of-service attacks can also affect other limited resources in the host, such as memory or link capacity: an attacker can launch such an attack on the memory of the device by sending fragments that BIH will store for a given period, and if the number of fragments is large enough the memory of the host could be exhausted. BIH implementations MUST implement proper protection against such attacks, for instance by allocating a limited amount of memory for fragmented packet storage.

Attackers may also try to keep a binding state alive forever by sending periodic packets that refresh the state. To allow BIH to defend against such attacks, the implementation MAY choose not to extend the session entry lifetime for a specific entry upon the reception of packets for that entry through the external interface, although such an action would not allow one-way communication sessions to stay alive.

BIH operates in combination with the DNS and is therefore subject to the security considerations appropriate to the DNS mode in which it is operating, recursive or stub-resolver mode. BIH also has the potential to interfere with the functioning of DNSSEC, because BIH modifies DNS answers and DNSSEC is designed to detect such modifications and to treat modified answers as bogus.
sections.plainLanguage: Three things follow from translating inside the host. End-to-end IP security over the IP header cannot survive it. The local address pool is a small resource that an attacker can exhaust by making the host resolve many names. And because the answers are rewritten, a DNSSEC validator will treat them as tampered with.

sections.title: What Changed from RFC 2767 and RFC 3338
sections.content:
This document combines and obsoletes both RFC 2767 and RFC 3338. The changes mainly reflect the following.

  • Addresses of RFC 1918 used for synthesis. RFC 3338 used unassigned IPv4 addresses, for example 0.0.0.1 to 0.0.0.255, for synthetic IPv4 addresses. Those addresses should not have been used and that may cause problems with applications. It is preferable to use addresses defined in RFC 1918.
  • Support for reverse (PTR) DNS queries. Neither RFC 2767 nor RFC 3338 included support for reverse DNS queries. This document adds that support.
  • DNSSEC support. RFC 2767 did not include DNSSEC considerations, which are now included.
  • Architectural recommendation. This document recommends the socket API-layer implementation option over network layer translation, that is, it recommends the approach introduced in RFC 2767 over the approach of RFC 3338.
  • Standards-Track document. RFC 2767 is classified as an Informational RFC and RFC 3338 as an Experimental RFC. It was discussed and decided in the IETF that this technology should be on the Standards Track.
  • Set of other extensions and improvements. These include IPv4 and IPv6 address exclusion sets, host DNS cache considerations, ENR behaviour updates, updated security considerations, and updated examples and deployment scenarios.
sections.plainLanguage: The two earlier documents become one, and three things change for the better: the local addresses come from the private IPv4 range that programs already understand, reverse name lookups work, and the socket API version is the one recommended.

viz.caption: THE PARTS OF A BIH IMPLEMENTATION

items.title: Extension Name Resolver
items.text: Answers the application's name lookup, using real IPv4 addresses when there are any and synthetic ones otherwise.

items.title: Address mapper
items.text: Hands out local IPv4 addresses from a pool and remembers the pairing with the real IPv6 address.

items.title: Function mapper
items.text: Turns an IPv4 socket API call into the matching IPv6 call. Used in the socket API version.

items.title: Protocol translator
items.text: Converts IPv4 packets to IPv6 and back with the SIIT algorithm. Used in the network layer version.

messages.label: LOOKUP
messages.note: The application asks for the IPv4 address of a name.

messages.label: A AND AAAA
messages.note: The resolver looks up both record types.

messages.label: REQUEST
messages.note: A local IPv4 address is needed for the IPv6 address.

messages.label: SYNTHETIC
messages.note: The mapper assigns one and records the pairing.

messages.label: IPV4 ADDRESS
messages.note: The application receives the synthetic address and uses it.

viz.caption: THE FOUR SECURITY POINTS OF BIH

items.title: IPsec over the IP header
items.text: End-to-end verification fails, because the header is rewritten. UDP encapsulation can restore it.

items.title: Filtering
items.text: Endpoint-Independent Mapping is required, and the security comes from the filtering, not the mapping.

items.title: Resource exhaustion
items.text: The address pool and memory for fragments are limited; an attacker can aim at both.

items.title: DNSSEC
items.text: Rewritten answers fail validation, so the host's resolver should not validate A records while BIH runs.
